The Bakery Co-op That Outgrew Its Ovens

By Tunde Oyelaran | 28 September 2026

When the twelve members of Crumb & Co first rented a shared kitchen in 2021, they baked on Sundays only, selling loaves from a folding table outside the station. Five years later, the cooperative supplies forty cafés, and its two ovens now run almost around the clock.

The members, who each hold one vote regardless of how many hours they work, agreed in August to borrow £300,000 for a larger unit on the edge of town. It was not an easy decision, said founding member Priya Sandhu, because the group had always prided itself on never owing anyone money.

“We argued for three meetings straight,” she said. “In the end, the choice was to grow or to start turning customers away, and nobody wanted to tell a café owner we couldn’t help them.”

The new unit will hold four deck ovens and a proving room, and it should allow the cooperative to take on six more members by next summer. Local lenders were cautious at first, according to the group’s treasurer, but a regional fund for worker-owned firms agreed to cover half of the loan.

Not everyone is convinced the model will scale. Small cooperatives often struggle once they pass twenty members, said an economist at the University of Northfield, because decisions take longer and early members can feel crowded out. Crumb & Co says it plans to split into two teams, each with its own budget, to avoid that problem.

For now, the bakers are focused on moving day, which is set for the first week of November. The old kitchen will stay open for one more month, so that regular customers can still pick up their Sunday loaves.
